The `title` tooltip is set on a `disabled` `<button>`, but most browsers don’t display tooltips for disabled form controls. That means users may not be able to discover why insight generation is disabled (especially while `sync.serverVersion === null`). Consider moving the tooltip to a non-disabled wrapper (e.g. a surrounding `<span>`), and/or showing a small inline hint when `generationUnavailable` is true (like you do for `readOnly`).

This hide rule is earlier and has the same effective specificity as the existing `#thinking-toggle:checked ~ main .message.thinking-only { display: block; }` rule, so when a message has both `thinking-only` and `focused-hidden`, enabling both Focused and Thinking makes the later Thinking rule win and re-shows content that Focused mode is supposed to hide.

Including the shared `markdownToolNames` here adds `Skill` to the HTML tool-block regex, but `formatContentForExport` does not parse `[Skill: ...]...[/Skill]` blocks first. A skill block is now partially wrapped as a tool block and the closing marker is left visible, regressing HTML rendering for skill content.

Focused mode does not account for system-injected messages. The SPA removes hidden system messages before applying transcript filtering (`MessageList.svelte` filters with `!isSystemMessage`), but this branch still marks any `role == "user"` system message visible and assistant system messages can become the pending answer, so focused HTML can include system/progress records and even hide a real answer behind them.

Clarifying what I meant by adapter here: `sessionUsageResponse` is only the private HTTP response wrapper for the successful `200` body, not a replacement for `db.SessionUsage`. It embeds `db.SessionUsage` so the existing DB/CLI JSON tags remain the REST success contract, then adds the HTTP-only `server_running: true` field and normalizes `unpriced_models` to `[]` when the DB DTO has nil.

The separate `sessionUsageErrorResponse` types are only for the new coded error body. Those are small enough that they could be simplified or shared if preferred; the success wrapper is there to avoid changing `db.SessionUsage` just to carry a REST-only field.
this looks a lot like backing out pbjson's int64 parser ?
Given that we know the json is created from pbjson should we make these using pbstruct etc ?
This why test suggests that this is stored using a pb.Any ?

Yes, exactly that — these are protojson int64s. The sidecar JSON comes from the daemon's Connect-RPC service (`exa.language_server_pb.LanguageServerService`), so 64-bit counts arrive as strings per the proto3 JSON mapping. I kept the decode hand-rolled rather than using protojson for two reasons: decoding with real protojson needs generated types from a `.proto` we don't have (the daemon's schema is closed and unpublished — the field set here is known only empirically), and protojson is strict where this path deliberately wants tolerance: a malformed count must decode to 0 rather than fail the whole trajectory decode and lose the transcript. It would also pull in `google.golang.org/protobuf` as a new dependency; the repo currently has no protobuf deps.

Same constraint as the int64 thread: to marshal fixtures with protojson we'd have to author our own `.proto` approximating Google's closed schema, which would make the fixtures look authoritative when they're really still an empirical guess — and would add the protobuf module for tests only. The hand-written JSON here mirrors captured daemon output shape-for-shape (string-encoded counts included), which I think is the more honest fixture for a format we don't own. Happy to revisit if the schema ever gets published.

I checked — it's not an `Any`. The production fragment decodes as `field 1: varint 0, field 4: varint 2, field 5: 2-byte LEN, field 8: varint 1`, whereas a `google.protobuf.Any` always starts with field 1 as a length-delimited type_url (`type.googleapis.com/...`). So it's just an ordinary nested message that happened to land in the field-21/19 position the walk treats as a model-name candidate. The underlying issue is that without the schema the wire format can't distinguish a string from a sub-message (both wire type 2), and a nested message whose bytes are all < 0x80 passes `utf8.Valid` — hence the printable-text guard.

The design tension behind both roborev findings lives here: ownership is keyed on the mutable `machine` string. Drop `sess.Machine != "local"` to fix the local/local collision and you instead freeze a host that renamed `pg.machine_name`/hostname — its explicitly-named rows can never update again, and the "sync from the origin machine" warning fires *on* the origin. Keep it, and the headline case stays broken. So I'd avoid a one-line patch to either; they want solving together.

The primitive for a real fix already exists: `pushMarkerID()` (push.go:411) is a stable per-local-DB id that survives renames and differs across machines — exactly the "stable owner marker" #655 hypothesized. Keying the decision on owner-identity rather than hostname resolves both directions. The schema-touching part is that `sessions` only stores `machine` today, not an owner id.

When this fires, the session is correctly left out of `pushed` — but it's also not reflected anywhere in `PushResult` (no skipped/conflict tally, `Errors` stays 0, the watermark advances). Combined with the guard's machine-name sensitivity, a misconfigured name can silently drop sessions with only a log line as signal. A `SkippedConflicts` counter would make it observable.

This is the second orphan-promotion implementation — the unpaginated path seeds orphans in the recursive CTE (`query_dialect.go`), while this paginated path promotes them here. That split is *why* the soft-deleted-parent divergence roborev caught exists at all. Rather than patch each path to match, I'd consolidate to a single shared canonical-root definition used by both paths — and, once the PG gap is closed, both backends — so they can't drift again.

Two small things here: this seed lists `'continuation'`, but continuations already surface as roots via the base `relationship_type NOT IN ('subagent','fork')`, so the token is redundant rather than load-bearing today. And it diverges from the canonical-root rule, which keys off `sidebarChildRelationshipsSQL` — another way the two promotion paths can drift. If continuations aren't meant to be promoted as orphans, drop it; otherwise reconcile both sides to one set.

These assert via `requireSessions` -> `ListSessions`, which routes through the CTE path — but the production paginated sidebar (`GetSidebarSessionIndex` with a `Limit`) goes through `buildCanonicalRootWhere`'s orphan branch, which no test exercises. So the shipping path (and the one that diverges) is unverified. Also worth adding: a nested orphan (an orphan subagent that itself has a child) to cover the recursive pull on a synthetic root, and a `continuation`-type orphan since the seed accepts it.

Unlike the sibling `CopyExcludedSessionsFrom`, this doesn't probe `sqlite_master` for the source table first. If an older local DB has no `pg_sync_state`, the `INSERT … SELECT` errors, and `ResyncAll` only logs-and-continues — so the marker isn't carried across the swap. The next push then generates a fresh marker and the machine forfeits ownership of every session it previously pushed, which is the exact failure this change is meant to prevent. Mirroring the existing `sqlite_master` probe (and maybe treating a marker-copy failure as fatal to the swap rather than log-and-continue) would close it.

Small residual of the same class you just fixed, continuation-only: the unpaginated root seed excludes just `sidebarChildRelationships` (subagent/fork), so a `continuation` whose parent exists-but-is-soft-deleted still seeds as a root here, while the paginated path (canonical set, includes continuation) correctly omits it. Net effect: a deleted parent's continuation child shows as a root in the no-limit sidebar but disappears in the paged one. Using `canonicalChildRelationships` for the unpaginated root seed (and this orphan seed) would make continuations consistent across both paths.

`DuckDBQueryDialect` leaves `canonicalChildRelationships` nil here — harmless today since DuckDB only goes through `BuildSessionFilterSQL`, but `CanonicalChildRelationshipsSQL()` would emit `relationship_type IN ()` if DuckDB ever picks up the canonical-root path. Relatedly, DuckDB is the third sidebar backend: `internal/duckdb/store.go` `GetSidebarSessionIndex` sets `IncludeChildren` but not `IncludeOrphans` (SQLite and PG both set it now), so orphan subagent/fork rows are dropped there. Setting `IncludeOrphans = true` in the DuckDB store and populating this dialect's canonical set to match keeps the third backend in parity.

This file is the snapshot generator/restorer tool, not the consumer. It needs to write files to disk (for `go generate`, restore from git artifacts, etc.), so `go:embed` isn't applicable here. The consumer side (`internal/pricing/fallback.go`) does use `go:embed` to bundle the generated snapshot into the binary:

```go
//go:embed snapshot/*

```

it seems super weird that you're not just using upsert.

Resolved in `b90a4ae`: the connection-kind branch now selects how mutation SQL is executed, not a separate write implementation. Local DuckDB keeps normal transaction execution, while Quack sends the same mutation SQL through `agentsview_remote.query(?)` so DuckDB plans it against the base tables instead of proxy tables.

Resolved in `b90a4ae`: sessions, model pricing, and cursor usage now keep their `ON CONFLICT` upserts. For Quack those upserts are executed server-side through the query hook, which preserves the intended conflict semantics while avoiding DuckDB proxy-table limitations. The dependent row sets still use the update/insert/delete path because DuckDB rejects delete-plus-reinsert of the same unique keys within one transaction.

Building the SQLite DSN by concatenating a raw filesystem path into a `file:` URI can break path resolution and even drop the `mode=ro` option when the path contains URI-reserved characters (notably `#` or `?`). In that case SQLite treats everything after `#` as a fragment, so the query parameters may be ignored and the DB may open read/write, undermining the read-only guarantee this PR relies on.

`sqliteWALHasFrames` currently returns false for any `os.Stat` error, which means a transient/permission/I/O stat failure will cause WAL write events to be treated as a handled no-op and the sync will be skipped. It’s safer to only treat `os.IsNotExist` as “no frames” and assume “has frames” for other unexpected stat errors so real updates aren’t silently dropped.

Considered that, but int64 UnixNano is the established convention for mtimes across the provider boundary — `SourceFingerprint.MTimeNS` in the same file, `dbBackedSessionMeta.FileMtime`, and `discoveredFileMtime` on the consumer side are all int64 nanos. A `time.Time` here would be the only one in the pipeline and would need conversion at both the producer (assigned from `meta.FileMtime`) and the consumer (compared against other int64 mtimes in the `--limit` sort). The `NS` suffix and the "zero means unset" sentinel follow the existing `MTimeNS` pattern. Happy to do a pipeline-wide `time.Time` conversion as a separate change if we want that convention instead.

> **AI Review Response** · Commit: 101c8774 · By: Claude Code with Opus 5

Good catch on the wording — the comment promised more than the code delivers, so
I've scoped it rather than rerouting the other caller.

The remaining direct call site is the incremental-append hash refresh
(`engine.go`, guarded by `agent == Codex || agent == Claude`). That one

@mariusvniekerk Is this what you mean by the write fix?

This gate still suppresses the pending global link whenever the reconciliation records a processing failure. Cached source failures deliberately remain `stats.Failed`, so if an unrelated malformed/missing source is still cached, the next unchanged poll skips this block and the failed scoped link is not retried; it can be deferred until that source recovers or the cache expires. The pending-link retry needs to be scheduled independently of per-source processing failures (while retaining the existing tombstone safety rules).

This classifier only recognizes `encoding/json/v2` error types, but providers also report malformed input as plain errors. For example, `ParseGrokSummary` returns `fmt.Errorf("decode ...: invalid json")` after `gjson.ValidBytes` (and Codebuff does the same), so those deterministic parse failures bypass this cache and continue to be reparsed and logged on every poll despite the documented malformed-data suppression. Use a shared typed malformed-data error or otherwise cover these provider error forms.

> **AI Review Response** · Commit: 254c5081 · By: Claude Code with Opus 5.5

Fixed in 254c5081. The branch now uses upstream's failure cache from #1833, so a cached source failure comes back as a skip rather than a counted failure. It no longer holds `stats.Failed` above zero, and the pending global link runs on the next poll. `TestPollingRetriesFailedLinkDespiteCachedSourceFailure` covers this case: a broken Gemini source stays cached while a failed Claude link is retried and repaired.

A source that fails without being cached, such as a permission error, still aborts the reconcile page, and linking waits until a pass has no failed page writes. Upstream behaves the same way, so this PR leaves it unchanged.

> **AI Review Response** · Commit: 254c5081 · By: Claude Code with Opus 5.5

This comment no longer applies after 254c5081. The branch dropped `source_failure_cache.go` and uses upstream's failure cache from #1833 instead. Upstream decides what to cache by the error message, and markers like "invalid" and "malformed" count as cacheable. So Grok's `decode ...: invalid json` and Codebuff's invalid-JSON errors are now cached and skipped until the source changes.

Could we avoid rebuilding the full search index for each page that changes messages? Each batch creates its own FTS suspender; [`Restore`](https://github.com/pascalwhoop/agentsview/blob/2d934ba8d7c5fce584400a3857560817ccc16a1c/internal/importer/importer.go#L91-L102) then [rebuilds the index for the entire archive](https://github.com/pascalwhoop/agentsview/blob/2d934ba8d7c5fce584400a3857560817ccc16a1c/internal/db/db.go#L3897-L3913), including existing sessions. Could we measure the cost across several changed pages on a populated archive, and check whether incremental indexing would preserve search availability without these repeated rebuilds?

Like all remaining release-side notes: v6.0.0 runs on Node 24 and requires Actions Runner >= 2.327.1. Not an issue for this repo, since the CI runner policy keeps every job on standard GitHub-hosted runners, which are always up to date - this only matters if someone runs this workflow on a self-hosted runner (e.g. a fork doing so would fail or emit warnings until runners are updated).

Quick note on this wrapper `<div class="markdown">`, since it looks redundant. The `.markdown :global(...)` rules in this file are scoped by Svelte, so they only match a `.markdown` element in this component's own template. `SkillBlock`'s own `.markdown` div carries its own scope class, so none of these rules reached it and the skill body rendered unstyled. Wrapping it here gives it the same prose styles as a normal message without duplicating CSS.

It's a bit of a workaround. A shared `<Markdown>` component, or moving these rules to a global stylesheet, would fix this cleanly, since several other places that call `renderMarkdown` use their own wrapper classes too. I didn't want to widen the scope of this PR, but I'm happy to follow up if that sounds useful.
